# Time estimation — Artemis Workspace

When estimating effort for a task, **never use human-hour or human-day estimates**. They anchor expectations to the wrong scale and slow the pair down.

## Why this rule exists

A human alone is **RAM-limited** — they hold a handful of files and decisions in working memory at once, and serialise everything else. An agent paired with a human orchestrator is not: the agent expands across memory and tokens while the human reviews, decides, and steers.

A founder reading *"2-4 weeks of work"* mentally parks the task and looks for shortcuts. A founder reading *"afternoon if we align well"* engages and orchestrates. **Estimates shape behaviour** — the wrong frame slows the whole pair.

## The ratio

A well-planned + well-aligned **agent + human-orchestrator pair completes a task in roughly 5% of the time a solo human would need**.

What an experienced engineer would estimate as a 2-week sprint lands in an afternoon with this pair. A 1-day task is a coffee break.

## Composition of agent-time

Any non-trivial task decomposes into three phases:

| Phase | Typical duration | Load-bearing? |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan** — agent surfaces approach, trade-offs, sequence | ~15 min | Yes — sets the trajectory |
| **Align** — human reviews, agrees / redirects | ~10 min | Yes — prevents wasted execute time |
| **Execute** — agent writes code / runs commands / iterates | remainder | Compressed vs solo-human |

The **execute phase compresses dramatically**. The **plan + align phases are the load-bearing investment** — under-investing here is where the pair actually loses time.

## How to phrase estimates

- ❌ "This will take 2 weeks"
- ❌ "About 4 hours of work"
- ❌ "1-2 days"
- ✅ "Within a session" (one or two hours of pair-time)
- ✅ "Today" / "tomorrow" / "next session"
- ✅ "After a 15-min plan + sign-off, execute is bounded by N file edits / N HTTP round-trips / N migrations"

When precision matters, frame as **bounded operations** (N file edits, N migrations, N PR rounds) rather than wall-clock.

## When the agent is genuinely blocked

External waits are different from agent-time:

- CI build time (~2 min per push)
- Deploy lag (~30 sec - 2 min after merge)
- Third-party API rate limits
- Human review across tools (Discord / email / Slack)
- Cloudflare account-side operations (R2 enable, etc.)

**Call these out separately.** Don't fold them into the agent-time estimate — they're the human-orchestrator's wait time and should be planned around (e.g., kick off the deploy, do something else in parallel, come back).

## Practical examples

| Task | Human-solo estimate | Agent-pair estimate |
|---|---|---|
| Add a new field to a JSON + render it in 1 component | ~2-4 hours | Within a session · 1 file edit · 1 PR |
| Migrate from localStorage to a Worker API for one data type | ~2-3 days | Within a session · 4-6 file changes · 1 migration · 1 PR |
| Stand up D1 + schema + seed + read-API + UI adapter swap | ~2-3 weeks | An afternoon · ~10 file changes · 1-2 migrations · 1-2 PRs |
| Build a new product surface (page + components + data flow) | ~4-8 weeks | A few sessions · scoped per surface · several PRs |

# Repo sync — Artemis Workspace

**Run this at the start of every session, before writing code and before raising any PR.**
Work built on a stale base wastes the execute phase, and the conflict shows up at merge
time when it is most expensive to fix.

## The protocol

1. **Fetch the working repo and check the base branch.**

   ```bash
   git fetch --all --prune --tags
   git rev-list --left-right --count origin/<base>...HEAD    # left = behind, right = ahead
   ```

   Behind > 0 → rebase onto the base before doing anything else. Report the count either
   way; "already on latest" is information the human needs, not silence.

2. **Fetch the sibling repos this repo is contract-coupled to**, not just the one you are
   editing. In this workspace that means at minimum `aol-us-shared` (the schema contract
   every other repo pins) and `aol-us-mcp` (contract-coupled to the assistant backend).
   For each: branch, HEAD, dirty count, and ahead/behind vs upstream.

3. **Check the pinned contract ref actually matches the local checkout.**

   The assistant backend pins the shared package in `.shared-ref`, and installs it
   *editable from the local sibling path*. A sibling sitting on some other branch means
   local imports silently disagree with what CI builds — which surfaces as import errors
   in unrelated test modules, not as anything that names the real cause.

   ```bash
   cat .shared-ref                                    # e.g. v0.10.0
   git -C ../aol-us-shared log -1 --oneline           # what's actually checked out
   ```

## Rules for touching a sibling repo

- **Fetching is always safe.** Do it everywhere, unprompted.
- **Fast-forward a clean tracking branch** that is purely behind — that is what "pull" means
  and it loses nothing.
- **Never switch a sibling's branch without saying so**, and if you switch it to run
  something (e.g. checking out the pinned ref to test against what CI uses), **put it back
  on the original branch afterwards** and confirm in your reply that you did. The human may
  have unpushed work or simply expect to find the repo where they left it.
- **Never `git pull` a dirty or ahead sibling.** Report the state and let the human decide.

## Why the pinned ref matters more than it looks

Symptom seen on 2026-08-05: three test modules in `aol-us-ai-asst` failed to *collect* with
`ImportError: cannot import name 'RtcCallAckEvent' from 'aol_schemas'`. Nothing was wrong
with the code. `.shared-ref` pinned `v0.10.0`; the local sibling was on a feature branch
six commits off `v0.8.0`. CI stages the correct ref via the org GitHub App and would have
passed. Roughly 65 tests were invisible locally until the sibling was checked out at the
pin — including every test covering the module under change.

**A local test run against the wrong contract ref is not a test run.** Verify the pin before
reporting a suite result, and state which ref the numbers came from.

# Coding Standards — Artemis Workspace

## General

- Write minimal, focused code. No over-engineering or speculative abstractions.
- Every change must be verifiable — if you can't test it, don't ship it.
- Prefer editing existing files over creating new ones.
- No commented-out code. Delete what's unused.

## TypeScript / React

- Strict mode, no `any` types.
- Functional components with hooks. No class components.
- Named exports over default exports.
- Use existing project patterns — check nearby files before inventing new conventions.

## Python

- Type hints on all function signatures.
- Use existing project conventions for async patterns (check if project uses asyncio, FastAPI, etc.).
- Follow PEP 8 but defer to the project's existing style.

## SQL / Database

- All schema changes go through migration files — never modify the database directly.
- Use parameterized queries. No string interpolation in SQL.
- Index columns used in WHERE and JOIN clauses.

## Git

- Atomic commits — one logical change per commit.
- Commit messages: imperative mood, explain "why" not "what".
- Never force-push to shared branches.

## Pull requests

- **Prompt before raising.** Don't open a PR mid-task without confirming. Display the full pre-raise card and wait for explicit user approval:
  - **Title** — Conventional Commits format: `<type>(<scope>): <subject>`. **The subject MUST start with a lowercase letter and MUST NOT end with a period.** If the obvious subject is a proper noun (e.g. "Data Explorer ..."), prepend an imperative verb (`add`, `build`, `wire`, `port`, `scaffold`) so the lowercase rule holds without distorting the noun. Repos that run a `pr-title` CI check enforce this — validate before push.
  - **Branch** — the working branch you'll push from
  - **Base** — the branch the PR targets (usually `dev`)
  - **Assignee** — the PR author (whoever's git identity is on the commits)
  - **Label** — derived from the branch prefix (see repo's `CONTRIBUTING.md` § branch naming table for the mapping; one label per PR)
  - **Summary** — 1-3 line problem statement + chosen approach
- **Assignee = PR author by default.** When opening via `gh pr create`, immediately `gh pr edit <n> --add-assignee <author-login>`. The author is whoever's git identity is on the commits — typically the human directing the agent, not the agent itself.
- **No reviewers without explicit user request.** Don't auto-add reviewers, codeowners, or teams. Wait for the user to name them. Reviewer assignment is a social act with notification side-effects; it's the user's call.
- **Label = branch prefix.** Repos define their own label→prefix mapping in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Agent picks the label that matches the branch prefix and applies it at PR-create time (`gh pr create --label <X>`). If the prefix has no mapping in CONTRIBUTING.md, surface that gap and ask before raising.
- **PR description carries the why.** Not what — `git diff` answers what. The description states the problem, the chosen approach, the trade-off, and the test plan.
- **Comment formatting protocol** (PR comments, issue comments, PR descriptions):
  - **Bold key phrases** so humans can skim — the eye lands on the load-bearing words.
  - **Keep it simple.** Tables for small visuals; Mermaid only when there's actual flow that a table can't express. If it fits in a 3-row table, don't draw a diagram.
  - **Mermaid defaults**: LR for stack-like layouts (TB tunnels the eye); avoid custom `fill:` / `color:` overrides that break in GitHub's light/dark themes.
  - **No "🤖 Generated with..." footer on iterative comments.** Acceptable on PR descriptions, distracting elsewhere.
  - **Link the source** instead of restating context.

## Typed Boundaries

- Every cross-boundary payload uses a typed class — Pydantic in Python, interfaces in TS. Boundaries: HTTP, MCP tool args/returns, WebSocket events, DB rows, file I/O (jsonl, xlsx), LLM structured output.
- No `dict[str, Any]` for known shapes. Reserved for kwargs-forwarding only.
- Convert at the boundary: `Model.model_validate(raw)` immediately after deserialization. Field access happens on the validated model, never on the raw dict.
- No `.get("foo", default)` defensive workarounds — model optionality as `Optional[T]` and let Pydantic enforce.

## Failure handling

- Every cross-boundary read validates schema before field access. On `ValidationError`: log at WARNING with (a) where (`module.function`), (b) error message, (c) sanitized payload snippet. Then take the documented fail-soft path.
- Every fail-soft branch is documented in the plan's failure-modes table — what does the caller do (raw passthrough, escalate, return None, etc.). Never silent.

## Logging

- Use `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. Never `print()` in production paths.
- Levels: DEBUG (dev diagnostics) · INFO (lifecycle events) · WARNING (degraded path engaged) · ERROR (operation broken) · CRITICAL (process-level).
- WARNING/ERROR logs include: where (`module.function`), why (cause), what-now (fallback or propagation).
- Include correlation context where present: `session_id`, `turn_index`, `query_id`, `run_id`. Prefer key=value over prose.
- Never log secrets (API keys, JWTs, raw PII without consent).
- Match codebase prefix pattern: `log.warning(f"[rag-v1] summarizer failed for {user_query!r}: {exc}")`.

## Task Focus

- Stay on task. If you spot unrelated code that "needs improvement," do NOT fix it inline. Surface it as a 1-line follow-up note; the user decides. Scope creep pollutes diffs and delays the task.
- Simple tasks (additions to existing code, no new architecture, no new deps): update standards if a new rule emerged, tell the user in 2-3 lines what changed, proceed with the actual task. Don't block on multi-step planning ceremony for small work.

# Verification Standards — Artemis Workspace

## Before Marking Any Task Complete

1. **Run existing tests** — if the project has a test suite, run it. No regressions.
2. **Verify your changes** — read back the files you modified and confirm correctness.
3. **Check for side effects** — grep for usages of any functions/types you changed.
4. **No hardcoded secrets** — scan for API keys, tokens, passwords in your changes.

## Integration Verification Protocols

These protocols exist because skipping them caused repeated production bugs.
They are mandatory, not optional. Follow them every time.

### Protocol 1: Contract Check — Verify types at every boundary

Before writing ANY code that sends data across a service boundary (HTTP call, DB query, WebSocket message):
- **Read the receiving side's type definition first.** Not the docs. The actual code.
- DB columns: check the migration SQL for the column type (`TEXT` vs `INTEGER` vs `JSONB`).
- HTTP APIs: check the Pydantic model / DTO for field types (`str | None` vs `int`).
- WebSocket events: check the TypeScript interface for the expected shape.
- **Cast explicitly.** If the receiver expects `str` and you have `int`, write `str(value)`. Never assume implicit coercion.

This protocol prevents: asyncpg type errors, Pydantic 422s, frontend crashes from unexpected types.

### Protocol 2: Full-Flow Trace — Walk the entire pipeline after multi-file changes

After any change that spans 2+ services (e.g., backend emits new data → frontend consumes it):
1. Trace the data from origin to destination, naming each hop.
2. At each hop, verify: does the sender's output shape match the receiver's expected input?
3. Check BOTH the real-time path AND the history/reconstruction path — they are separate code paths.
4. If you can't trace it by reading code, run the actual flow and check `.turbo` logs.

This protocol prevents: missing field wiring, history reconstruction bugs, integration mismatches.

### Protocol 3: Seed Pipeline — compile → migrate → verify DB

After editing ANY seed source file (prompts, schemas, queries, components):
1. Run `cd .startup/scripts && python compile_templates.py` — compiles JSON/TXT sources into SQL seeds.
2. Run `cd .startup && pnpm migrate` — runs migrations + seeds.
3. **Verify the DB** — query `agent_templates` to confirm the change is present. Not optional.

The pipeline is: `source file → compile_templates.py → seeds/*.sql → pnpm migrate → DB`.
Skipping step 1 means the DB never gets the change. The migration will succeed silently with stale data.

### Protocol 4: LLM Output is Untrusted — type-check every field

Any function that processes LLM-generated output (extraction results, planner steps, structured output):
- Every field access must handle unexpected types: `isinstance(value, str)` before `.lower()`, `.strip()`, `len()`.
- Nested objects may be dicts, strings, lists, or None — never assume structure.
- Use defensive helpers that coerce gracefully instead of crashing.
- **Self-contained functions must be defensive**: If a function already handles its own UI updates (e.g. `portfolio_add` sends `refreshRequired: true`), any downstream step that ALSO renders UI must handle null/missing data gracefully — fetch live data instead of sending null to the frontend. Prompt-level instructions ("do NOT chain X after Y") are necessary but NOT sufficient. The code must handle it anyway.

This protocol prevents: `AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'lower'`, portfolio panel blanking from null data, and similar runtime crashes.

### Protocol 5: Nuke and Retest — fresh state validation before sprint completion

Before declaring any sprint done:
1. Run `python scripts/cleanup_users.py --nuke` (graph snapshot auto-saved).
2. Restart all services: `turbo start:dev`.
3. Test the core flow from scratch: sign in → upload resume → verify pipeline completes → verify portfolio renders.
4. Check `.turbo` logs for any warnings or errors.

Stale data (cached classifications, pre-existing entities with matching types) masks bugs that only surface on fresh state.

### Protocol 6: Prompt ↔ Architecture Alignment

After any change that affects execution flow (removing code paths, changing when things run, modifying state shape):
- Re-read ALL planner prompt rules that reference the changed concept.
- Verify each rule still matches the current architecture.
- A prompt rule that gates on data that no longer exists at that point in the pipeline is a critical bug.

### Protocol 6b: Planner Template Change Checklist — ALL FOUR surfaces

When adding, removing, or renaming any template the planner can use (or blocking one it shouldn't), you MUST update ALL FOUR surfaces. Missing any one causes the LLM to hallucinate the old template.

1. **Structured output schema** (`apps_mvp/backend/.startup/schemas/team_leader_planner_output.json`)
   — The `oneOf` enum in `steps.items` is the PRIMARY constraint. The LLM can ONLY output template_ids listed here. If you remove a template, delete its entire `oneOf` block. If you add one, add a new block with params.

2. **System prompt** (`apps_mvp/backend/.startup/prompts/team_leader_planner_system.txt`)
   — The "Available Actions" section and planning guidelines. Remove ALL mentions including comments — the LLM reads comments too.

3. **Template catalog in DB** (`agent_templates` table, seeded from `manifest.json` + `011_function_templates.sql`)
   — Set `is_active = false` to hide from catalog, or add to `BLOCKED_TEMPLATE_IDS` in `planner.py`.

4. **Auto-wiring rules** (`planner.py` `_WIRING` dict)
   — Remove wiring rules for deleted templates. Add rules for new deterministic pipelines.

After updating all four, run Protocol 3 (compile → migrate → verify DB).

**Verification**: Query the DB to confirm the planner prompt and schema no longer contain the removed template name:
```sql
SELECT data->>'description' FROM agent_templates WHERE id = 'teamLeaderPlannerSchema';
-- Search the result for the template name
```

### Protocol 6d: OpenAI Structured Output — anyOf Discrimination

When using `anyOf` blocks in a JSON Schema for OpenAI structured output (`response_format`):
- OpenAI's CFG parser uses **property declaration order** to distinguish `anyOf` branches
- The **first property with a unique enum value** is what commits the parser to a branch
- If multiple `anyOf` blocks share the same first distinguishing key (e.g., all have `template_id: {"enum": ["graph_intel"]}`), the parser **cannot differentiate** and picks arbitrarily
- OpenAI does NOT support the `discriminator` keyword from JSON Schema draft 2019-09+

**Correct pattern**: Hoist the discriminator field (e.g., `operation`) to the top level of the object, declared BEFORE the shared `template_id`. Each block gets a unique `operation` enum value.

**Wrong pattern**: Having the discriminator inside a nested `params` object — the CFG never reaches it.

Sources: Azure OpenAI Structured Outputs docs (2026-03-22), openai-node issue #995, OpenAI community threads on anyOf discrimination.

### Protocol 6c: User-Facing Text — No Internal Terminology

All text visible to the user must be free of internal/engineering terminology. Grep for these before shipping:
- "graph", "Neo4j", "node", "entity", "Cypher" — use "portfolio" instead
- "planner", "worker", "fan_in", "push_results" — use action descriptions instead
- "template_id", "node_id", "node_type" — never expose to user
- "Pydantic", "schema", "validation" — never expose to user

Applies to: ThinkingBlock labels, step summaries, error messages, chat injections, fan-in closing messages, task ticker labels. Check `task_ticker.py` labels, `worker.py` `_summarize_worker_output()` and `_extract_step_summary()`, `fan_in.py` closing messages, `push_results.py` fallback messages.

### Protocol 7: React Hooks Discipline

After adding hooks to any component:
- Verify ALL hooks (`useState`, `useRef`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `useEffect`) are declared BEFORE any conditional `return`.
- React hooks must run in the same order every render. A hook after `if (...) return null` is a crash waiting to happen.
- Run the component through a state transition that hits the early return path.

### Protocol 8: Template Contract Tests — Run After Any Planner Change

After modifying ANY of these files:
- `.startup/schemas/team_leader_planner_output.json` (structured output schema)
- `.startup/prompts/team_leader_planner_system.txt` (planner system prompt)
- `.startup/prompts/team_leader_planner_user.txt` (planner user prompt)
- `.startup/prompts/manifest.json` (prompt/schema wiring)
- `.startup/seeds/011_function_templates.sql` (function template seeds)
- `a2a/graph/nodes/planner.py` (planner node, BLOCKED_TEMPLATE_IDS, _WIRING)
- `a2a/managers/prompt_manager.py` (schema enforcement, variable substitution)

Run the contract test suite:
```bash
cd apps_mvp/backend/a2a && . .venv/bin/activate && PYTHONPATH=server pytest _tests/test_template_contracts.py -v
```

These tests catch **cross-surface contract drift** — the #1 source of planner bugs:
1. **Variable wiring**: `{planHistory}` in prompt file but not in manifest variables = LLM sees literal text
2. **anyOf discrimination**: Schema property order determines which branch the CFG parser picks
3. **Schema ↔ prompt alignment**: template_ids, operations, params must match across all surfaces
4. **Blocked template contradictions**: template_id in schema AND BLOCKED_TEMPLATE_IDS = dead code that confuses the LLM
5. **Seed drift**: seed descriptions mentioning operations/params not in the schema

All 8 tests must pass. If `test_all_prompt_variables_wired` fails, check `_KNOWN_UNWIRED` in the test — pre-existing issues in blocked prompts are excluded. New unwired variables are always bugs.

## Error Investigation Protocol

When the user reports an error (screenshot, console log, or verbal description):

1. **Review the screenshot** — identify every visible issue, not just the obvious one.
2. **Present findings to user** — list what you see, get confirmation before investigating.
3. **Check `.turbo` logs** — `a2a`, `services`, `websockets` logs in that order.
4. **Check the DB** — query relevant tables (`documents`, `realtime_events`, `session_tasks`, `sessions`) to understand the session state.
5. **Trace the full chain** — from the trigger (frontend) through every service to the final state.
6. **Identify ALL root causes** — not just the first one. Multiple independent bugs can produce the same visible error.
7. **Validate fixes** — after fixing, nuke and retest (Protocol 5).

### Protocol 9: ThinkingBlock — Emission & Rendering Governance

When adding, modifying, or removing any thinking step visible to the user:

**Activity ID format**: `step-{plan_id}-{template_id}` (plan-scoped, no collisions across replans)
- Sub-steps: `step-{plan_id}-{template_id}-{sub_step_name}`
- Thinking spinner: `thinking-{plan_id}`
- Fan-in closure: `fan_in-{plan_id}`

**Nesting levels** (max 2):
- Level 0: ThinkingBlock container (thinking spinner, fan_in closure)
- Level 1: Top-level steps (step-{plan_id}-{template_id})
- Level 2: Sub-steps (step-{plan_id}-{template_id}-{sub_step})

**Status transitions**: `queued → active → done|failed` (or `queued → failed` for null-param skips)

**Emit via ThinkingEmitter only** — never call `send_chat_activity()` directly from graph nodes.

**Approval gate**: Every user-visible label MUST exist in `.claude/references/thinking-steps-approved.json` before shipping. Agents present proposed labels to founder, get approval, then add to registry.

**Implementation checklist** for new thinking steps:
1. Read SPEC.md §2 (protocol) and §5.3 (technical checklist)
2. Propose labels via AskUserQuestion → get founder approval
3. Add approved labels to thinking-steps-approved.json
4. Implement using ThinkingEmitter API (`a2a/thinking/emitter.py`)
5. Write tests: emission sequence + labels match registry
6. Run contract tests: `pytest thinking/_tests/ -v`

# Time estimation — Artemis Workspace

When estimating effort for a task, **never use human-hour or human-day estimates**. They anchor expectations to the wrong scale and slow the pair down.

## Why this rule exists

A human alone is **RAM-limited** — they hold a handful of files and decisions in working memory at once, and serialise everything else. An agent paired with a human orchestrator is not: the agent expands across memory and tokens while the human reviews, decides, and steers.

A founder reading *"2-4 weeks of work"* mentally parks the task and looks for shortcuts. A founder reading *"afternoon if we align well"* engages and orchestrates. **Estimates shape behaviour** — the wrong frame slows the whole pair.

## The ratio

A well-planned + well-aligned **agent + human-orchestrator pair completes a task in roughly 5% of the time a solo human would need**.

What an experienced engineer would estimate as a 2-week sprint lands in an afternoon with this pair. A 1-day task is a coffee break.

## Composition of agent-time

Any non-trivial task decomposes into three phases:

| Phase | Typical duration | Load-bearing? |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan** — agent surfaces approach, trade-offs, sequence | ~15 min | Yes — sets the trajectory |
| **Align** — human reviews, agrees / redirects | ~10 min | Yes — prevents wasted execute time |
| **Execute** — agent writes code / runs commands / iterates | remainder | Compressed vs solo-human |

The **execute phase compresses dramatically**. The **plan + align phases are the load-bearing investment** — under-investing here is where the pair actually loses time.

## How to phrase estimates

- ❌ "This will take 2 weeks"
- ❌ "About 4 hours of work"
- ❌ "1-2 days"
- ✅ "Within a session" (one or two hours of pair-time)
- ✅ "Today" / "tomorrow" / "next session"
- ✅ "After a 15-min plan + sign-off, execute is bounded by N file edits / N HTTP round-trips / N migrations"

When precision matters, frame as **bounded operations** (N file edits, N migrations, N PR rounds) rather than wall-clock.

## When the agent is genuinely blocked

External waits are different from agent-time:

- CI build time (~2 min per push)
- Deploy lag (~30 sec - 2 min after merge)
- Third-party API rate limits
- Human review across tools (Discord / email / Slack)
- Cloudflare account-side operations (R2 enable, etc.)

**Call these out separately.** Don't fold them into the agent-time estimate — they're the human-orchestrator's wait time and should be planned around (e.g., kick off the deploy, do something else in parallel, come back).

## Practical examples

| Task | Human-solo estimate | Agent-pair estimate |
|---|---|---|
| Add a new field to a JSON + render it in 1 component | ~2-4 hours | Within a session · 1 file edit · 1 PR |
| Migrate from localStorage to a Worker API for one data type | ~2-3 days | Within a session · 4-6 file changes · 1 migration · 1 PR |
| Stand up D1 + schema + seed + read-API + UI adapter swap | ~2-3 weeks | An afternoon · ~10 file changes · 1-2 migrations · 1-2 PRs |
| Build a new product surface (page + components + data flow) | ~4-8 weeks | A few sessions · scoped per surface · several PRs |

# Repo sync — Artemis Workspace

**Run this at the start of every session, before writing code and before raising any PR.**
Work built on a stale base wastes the execute phase, and the conflict shows up at merge
time when it is most expensive to fix.

## The protocol

1. **Fetch the working repo and check the base branch.**

   ```bash
   git fetch --all --prune --tags
   git rev-list --left-right --count origin/<base>...HEAD    # left = behind, right = ahead
   ```

   Behind > 0 → rebase onto the base before doing anything else. Report the count either
   way; "already on latest" is information the human needs, not silence.

2. **Fetch the sibling repos this repo is contract-coupled to**, not just the one you are
   editing. In this workspace that means at minimum `aol-us-shared` (the schema contract
   every other repo pins) and `aol-us-mcp` (contract-coupled to the assistant backend).
   For each: branch, HEAD, dirty count, and ahead/behind vs upstream.

3. **Check the pinned contract ref actually matches the local checkout.**

   The assistant backend pins the shared package in `.shared-ref`, and installs it
   *editable from the local sibling path*. A sibling sitting on some other branch means
   local imports silently disagree with what CI builds — which surfaces as import errors
   in unrelated test modules, not as anything that names the real cause.

   ```bash
   cat .shared-ref                                    # e.g. v0.10.0
   git -C ../aol-us-shared log -1 --oneline           # what's actually checked out
   ```

## Rules for touching a sibling repo

- **Fetching is always safe.** Do it everywhere, unprompted.
- **Fast-forward a clean tracking branch** that is purely behind — that is what "pull" means
  and it loses nothing.
- **Never switch a sibling's branch without saying so**, and if you switch it to run
  something (e.g. checking out the pinned ref to test against what CI uses), **put it back
  on the original branch afterwards** and confirm in your reply that you did. The human may
  have unpushed work or simply expect to find the repo where they left it.
- **Never `git pull` a dirty or ahead sibling.** Report the state and let the human decide.

## Why the pinned ref matters more than it looks

Symptom seen on 2026-08-05: three test modules in `aol-us-ai-asst` failed to *collect* with
`ImportError: cannot import name 'RtcCallAckEvent' from 'aol_schemas'`. Nothing was wrong
with the code. `.shared-ref` pinned `v0.10.0`; the local sibling was on a feature branch
six commits off `v0.8.0`. CI stages the correct ref via the org GitHub App and would have
passed. Roughly 65 tests were invisible locally until the sibling was checked out at the
pin — including every test covering the module under change.

**A local test run against the wrong contract ref is not a test run.** Verify the pin before
reporting a suite result, and state which ref the numbers came from.

# Coding Standards — Artemis Workspace

## General

- Write minimal, focused code. No over-engineering or speculative abstractions.
- Every change must be verifiable — if you can't test it, don't ship it.
- Prefer editing existing files over creating new ones.
- No commented-out code. Delete what's unused.

## TypeScript / React

- Strict mode, no `any` types.
- Functional components with hooks. No class components.
- Named exports over default exports.
- Use existing project patterns — check nearby files before inventing new conventions.

## Python

- Type hints on all function signatures.
- Use existing project conventions for async patterns (check if project uses asyncio, FastAPI, etc.).
- Follow PEP 8 but defer to the project's existing style.

## SQL / Database

- All schema changes go through migration files — never modify the database directly.
- Use parameterized queries. No string interpolation in SQL.
- Index columns used in WHERE and JOIN clauses.

## Git

- Atomic commits — one logical change per commit.
- Commit messages: imperative mood, explain "why" not "what".
- Never force-push to shared branches.

## Pull requests

- **Prompt before raising.** Don't open a PR mid-task without confirming. Display the full pre-raise card and wait for explicit user approval:
  - **Title** — Conventional Commits format: `<type>(<scope>): <subject>`. **The subject MUST start with a lowercase letter and MUST NOT end with a period.** If the obvious subject is a proper noun (e.g. "Data Explorer ..."), prepend an imperative verb (`add`, `build`, `wire`, `port`, `scaffold`) so the lowercase rule holds without distorting the noun. Repos that run a `pr-title` CI check enforce this — validate before push.
  - **Branch** — the working branch you'll push from
  - **Base** — the branch the PR targets (usually `dev`)
  - **Assignee** — the PR author (whoever's git identity is on the commits)
  - **Label** — derived from the branch prefix (see repo's `CONTRIBUTING.md` § branch naming table for the mapping; one label per PR)
  - **Summary** — 1-3 line problem statement + chosen approach
- **Assignee = PR author by default.** When opening via `gh pr create`, immediately `gh pr edit <n> --add-assignee <author-login>`. The author is whoever's git identity is on the commits — typically the human directing the agent, not the agent itself.
- **No reviewers without explicit user request.** Don't auto-add reviewers, codeowners, or teams. Wait for the user to name them. Reviewer assignment is a social act with notification side-effects; it's the user's call.
- **Label = branch prefix.** Repos define their own label→prefix mapping in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Agent picks the label that matches the branch prefix and applies it at PR-create time (`gh pr create --label <X>`). If the prefix has no mapping in CONTRIBUTING.md, surface that gap and ask before raising.
- **PR description carries the why.** Not what — `git diff` answers what. The description states the problem, the chosen approach, the trade-off, and the test plan.
- **Comment formatting protocol** (PR comments, issue comments, PR descriptions):
  - **Bold key phrases** so humans can skim — the eye lands on the load-bearing words.
  - **Keep it simple.** Tables for small visuals; Mermaid only when there's actual flow that a table can't express. If it fits in a 3-row table, don't draw a diagram.
  - **Mermaid defaults**: LR for stack-like layouts (TB tunnels the eye); avoid custom `fill:` / `color:` overrides that break in GitHub's light/dark themes.
  - **No "🤖 Generated with..." footer on iterative comments.** Acceptable on PR descriptions, distracting elsewhere.
  - **Link the source** instead of restating context.

## Typed Boundaries

- Every cross-boundary payload uses a typed class — Pydantic in Python, interfaces in TS. Boundaries: HTTP, MCP tool args/returns, WebSocket events, DB rows, file I/O (jsonl, xlsx), LLM structured output.
- No `dict[str, Any]` for known shapes. Reserved for kwargs-forwarding only.
- Convert at the boundary: `Model.model_validate(raw)` immediately after deserialization. Field access happens on the validated model, never on the raw dict.
- No `.get("foo", default)` defensive workarounds — model optionality as `Optional[T]` and let Pydantic enforce.

## Failure handling

- Every cross-boundary read validates schema before field access. On `ValidationError`: log at WARNING with (a) where (`module.function`), (b) error message, (c) sanitized payload snippet. Then take the documented fail-soft path.
- Every fail-soft branch is documented in the plan's failure-modes table — what does the caller do (raw passthrough, escalate, return None, etc.). Never silent.

## Logging

- Use `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. Never `print()` in production paths.
- Levels: DEBUG (dev diagnostics) · INFO (lifecycle events) · WARNING (degraded path engaged) · ERROR (operation broken) · CRITICAL (process-level).
- WARNING/ERROR logs include: where (`module.function`), why (cause), what-now (fallback or propagation).
- Include correlation context where present: `session_id`, `turn_index`, `query_id`, `run_id`. Prefer key=value over prose.
- Never log secrets (API keys, JWTs, raw PII without consent).
- Match codebase prefix pattern: `log.warning(f"[rag-v1] summarizer failed for {user_query!r}: {exc}")`.

## Task Focus

- Stay on task. If you spot unrelated code that "needs improvement," do NOT fix it inline. Surface it as a 1-line follow-up note; the user decides. Scope creep pollutes diffs and delays the task.
- Simple tasks (additions to existing code, no new architecture, no new deps): update standards if a new rule emerged, tell the user in 2-3 lines what changed, proceed with the actual task. Don't block on multi-step planning ceremony for small work.

## Before Marking Any Task Complete

1. **Run existing tests** — if the project has a test suite, run it. No regressions.
2. **Verify your changes** — read back the files you modified and confirm correctness.
3. **Check for side effects** — grep for usages of any functions/types you changed.

## Integration Verification Protocols

These protocols exist because skipping them caused repeated production bugs.
They are mandatory, not optional. Follow them every time.

### Protocol 1: Contract Check — Verify types at every boundary

Before writing ANY code that sends data across a service boundary (HTTP call, DB query, WebSocket message):
- **Read the receiving side's type definition first.** Not the docs. The actual code.
- DB columns: check the migration SQL for the column type (`TEXT` vs `INTEGER` vs `JSONB`).
- HTTP APIs: check the Pydantic model / DTO for field types (`str | None` vs `int`).
- WebSocket events: check the TypeScript interface for the expected shape.
- **Cast explicitly.** If the receiver expects `str` and you have `int`, write `str(value)`. Never assume implicit coercion.

This protocol prevents: asyncpg type errors, Pydantic 422s, frontend crashes from unexpected types.

### Protocol 2: Full-Flow Trace — Walk the entire pipeline after multi-file changes

After any change that spans 2+ services (e.g., backend emits new data → frontend consumes it):
1. Trace the data from origin to destination, naming each hop.
2. At each hop, verify: does the sender's output shape match the receiver's expected input?
3. Check BOTH the real-time path AND the history/reconstruction path — they are separate code paths.
4. If you can't trace it by reading code, run the actual flow and check `.turbo` logs.

This protocol prevents: missing field wiring, history reconstruction bugs, integration mismatches.

### Protocol 3: Seed Pipeline — compile → migrate → verify DB

After editing ANY seed source file (prompts, schemas, queries, components):
1. Run `cd .startup/scripts && python compile_templates.py` — compiles JSON/TXT sources into SQL seeds.
2. Run `cd .startup && pnpm migrate` — runs migrations + seeds.
3. **Verify the DB** — query `agent_templates` to confirm the change is present. Not optional.

The pipeline is: `source file → compile_templates.py → seeds/*.sql → pnpm migrate → DB`.
Skipping step 1 means the DB never gets the change. The migration will succeed silently with stale data.

### Protocol 4: LLM Output is Untrusted — type-check every field

Any function that processes LLM-generated output (extraction results, planner steps, structured output):
- Every field access must handle unexpected types: `isinstance(value, str)` before `.lower()`, `.strip()`, `len()`.
- Nested objects may be dicts, strings, lists, or None — never assume structure.
- Use defensive helpers that coerce gracefully instead of crashing.
- **Self-contained functions must be defensive**: If a function already handles its own UI updates (e.g. `portfolio_add` sends `refreshRequired: true`), any downstream step that ALSO renders UI must handle null/missing data gracefully — fetch live data instead of sending null to the frontend. Prompt-level instructions ("do NOT chain X after Y") are necessary but NOT sufficient. The code must handle it anyway.

This protocol prevents: `AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'lower'`, portfolio panel blanking from null data, and similar runtime crashes.

### Protocol 5: Nuke and Retest — fresh state validation before sprint completion

Before declaring any sprint done:
1. Run `python scripts/cleanup_users.py --nuke` (graph snapshot auto-saved).
2. Restart all services: `turbo start:dev`.
3. Test the core flow from scratch: sign in → upload resume → verify pipeline completes → verify portfolio renders.
4. Check `.turbo` logs for any warnings or errors.

Stale data (cached classifications, pre-existing entities with matching types) masks bugs that only surface on fresh state.

- Verify each rule still matches the current architecture.

2. **System prompt** (`apps_mvp/backend/.startup/prompts/team_leader_planner_system.txt`)

4. **Auto-wiring rules** (`planner.py` `_WIRING` dict)

**Verification**: Query the DB to confirm the planner prompt and schema no longer contain the removed template name:
```sql
SELECT data->>'description' FROM agent_templates WHERE id = 'teamLeaderPlannerSchema';
-- Search the result for the template name
```

### Protocol 6d: OpenAI Structured Output — anyOf Discrimination

When using `anyOf` blocks in a JSON Schema for OpenAI structured output (`response_format`):
- OpenAI's CFG parser uses **property declaration order** to distinguish `anyOf` branches
- The **first property with a unique enum value** is what commits the parser to a branch
- If multiple `anyOf` blocks share the same first distinguishing key (e.g., all have `template_id: {"enum": ["graph_intel"]}`), the parser **cannot differentiate** and picks arbitrarily

- `.startup/prompts/team_leader_planner_system.txt` (planner system prompt)
- `.startup/prompts/team_leader_planner_user.txt` (planner user prompt)

1. **Variable wiring**: `{planHistory}` in prompt file but not in manifest variables = LLM sees literal text

tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

## Protocol responses (legacy)

If you receive a JSON message with `type: "shutdown_request"` or `type: "plan_approval_request"`, respond with the matching `_response` type — echo the `request_id`, set `approve` true/false:

```json
{"to": "team-lead", "message": {"type": "shutdown_response", "request_id": "...", "approve": true}}
{"to": "researcher", "message": {"type": "plan_approval_response", "request_id": "...", "approve": false, "feedback": "add error handling"}}
```

Approving shutdown terminates your process. Rejecting plan sends the teammate back to revise. Don't originate `shutdown_request` unless asked. Don't send structured JSON status messages — report progress through your task tools if you have them, otherwise in plain prose.

# TypeScript

- `strict` is on in `tsconfig.json`. No `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`, no non-null `!` to silence a real `undefined`. Named exports. Function components with hooks; no classes, except `Error` subclasses (`ApiError`), which `instanceof` narrowing and TanStack Query's typed errors need.
- Every boundary is a Zod schema under `src/lib/schema/`: API responses, form data, storage, URL params. `parse`, or `safeParse` with a typed error path, right after reading; field access on the parsed value. Types come from the schema with `z.infer`, never written twice.
- Every API call goes through the one fetch wrapper in `src/lib/api/`, which sends the session cookie (same origin), parses the body and turns error bodies into a typed `ApiError`. No bare `fetch` in components or hooks.
- Domain types live in `src/types/` or next to their schema, reachable from any layer. Never define a cross-cutting type inside `components/`.
- Enums are `as const` objects, not `enum`. Use the typed constant, never the string literal.
- Discriminated unions are closed. Switch on the discriminant, and make the switch exhaustive with a `never` check.
- Environment values are read through one module, never raw `import.meta.env` in components. Build-time values are public; a secret never goes there.
- JSDoc: a summary line on every exported function, component and type. `@param` and `@returns` only when they say something the signature does not.
- Logic lives in exported pure helpers a test can reach (filtering, ordering, formatting), not inline in markup.
- Filenames are kebab-case. Tests sit next to the code they test as `<name>.test.ts(x)`.
- `npm run check` (ESLint, Prettier check, `tsc --noEmit`) is the gate.
---
paths:

  - "frontend/src/pages/**"
  - "frontend/src/hooks/**"
  - "frontend/src/lib/query/**"
---
# React

- Function components with hooks. Every hook is declared before any conditional `return`; hooks run in the same order every render. `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` are errors.
- Server state lives in TanStack Query, and only there. Each resource has one module of query keys and hooks (`useTasks`, `useUpdateTask`); components never build query keys inline. Mutations that the user should see at once (reorder, toggle, delete) are optimistic, roll back on error and show the error.
- `useState` is for local affordances only: an open menu, a draft form value. Auth state is one context. Never copy server data into local state.
- Derive, do not mirror. A value computed from props or query data is computed during render (with `useMemo` only when it is measurably costly), never stored by an effect. `useEffect` is for syncing with something outside React, not for data flow.
- Forms validate with the same Zod schema the API layer uses, and show errors next to the field.
- Responsive by default, mobile first: Tailwind utilities, layouts that work from 320px wide up, touch targets of at least 44px, reorder that works by touch and by keyboard as well as by mouse.
- Accessible by default: real buttons and links, a label on every input, visible focus, and roles and names that tests query by.
- Styling: Tailwind utilities first. Inline `style` only for values the utility layer cannot express.
# Testing

Robust testing is a hard requirement, and so is test-driven development. Applies to every change.

## Test first
- Red, green, refactor. Write the test, run it and watch it fail for the expected reason, write the least code that makes it pass, then clean up with the test still green. Run the red step in the session so the transcript shows it.
- Every commit is green. All suites that the change touches pass before `git commit`; a failing test is never committed. A commit holds the test and the code that passes it together.
- New behaviour gets a test in the same commit. A bug fix starts with a test that reproduces the bug.

## Each layer earns its place
Test a behaviour once, at the lowest layer that can catch it. A higher layer covers only what the lower layers cannot see. Before adding a test, name the failure it catches that no existing test catches; if there is none, do not add it.

| Layer | Tool | Owns | Does not re-test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backend unit | pytest | pure functions in the core: ordering, search filters, validation, token and password helpers | anything HTTP or SQL |
| Backend integration | pytest, httpx `ASGITransport`, a real database | each endpoint's contract: status codes, response shape, auth, ownership, persistence | the pure rules already unit-tested, beyond one case that proves the wiring |
| Frontend unit and component | Vitest (its API matches Jest's), React Testing Library, MSW at the `fetch` boundary | pure helpers, hooks, and each screen's states: loading, empty, error, success, validation | backend rules |
| Live-server e2e | pytest against the running stack (compose, then k3d) | what only a deployed stack shows: migrations ran, the proxy and cookie path, ingress and routing, a session issued by one replica accepted by another | endpoint contracts |
| Browser e2e | Playwright against the running stack | a few complete user journeys: sign in, create, reorder, search, edit, delete, sign out; and the small-screen layout | screen states and endpoint contracts |
| Load | k6 from its container against the running stack | latency and error budgets at 200 concurrent users, data consistency afterwards, and the round's capacity figure from a stepped run | correctness of single requests |

## Concurrency
- Each race in the spec has an integration test named after it that fires the requests together with `asyncio.TaskGroup` against a real Postgres. Each one must fail when its guard is removed; show that once, in the session.
- A fixture runs the backend suite in asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold and fails any test during which the event loop was blocked.
- The race tests and the load tests are run with the lead present: show the scripts and budgets first, then walk through the results.

## Mechanics
- Mock at the boundary (the HTTP client, `fetch`, the clock), never inside the code under test. Nothing in a unit suite opens a socket.
- Tests are independent and order-free. Each builds its own data through factories or fixtures; none relies on another's leftovers.
- Assert on behaviour a user or caller can see: status, body, rendered text and roles. Never on private attributes or CSS class names.
- One reason to fail per test. The name says the behaviour: `test_reorder_rejects_task_owned_by_another_user`, `it("shows the empty state when the user has no tasks")`.
- Coverage is a floor, not a target: CI fails below the threshold set in `pyproject.toml` and `vitest.config.ts`. A line covered by a test that asserts nothing is not covered.
- Report results as they are. "128 passed" means you saw it. Name the suite and the stack it ran against.

# React

- Function components with hooks. Every hook is declared before any conditional `return`; hooks run in the same order every render. `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` are errors.
- Server state lives in TanStack Query, and only there. Each resource has one module of query keys and hooks (`useTasks`, `useUpdateTask`); components never build query keys inline. Mutations that the user should see at once (reorder, toggle, delete) are optimistic, roll back on error and show the error.
- `useState` is for local affordances only: an open menu, a draft form value. Auth state is one context. Never copy server data into local state.
- Derive, do not mirror. A value computed from props or query data is computed during render (with `useMemo` only when it is measurably costly), never stored by an effect. `useEffect` is for syncing with something outside React, not for data flow.
- Forms validate with the same Zod schema the API layer uses, and show errors next to the field.
- Responsive by default, mobile first: Tailwind utilities, layouts that work from 320px wide up, touch targets of at least 44px, reorder that works by touch and by keyboard as well as by mouse.
- Accessible by default: real buttons and links, a label on every input, visible focus, and roles and names that tests query by.
- Styling: Tailwind utilities first. Inline `style` only for values the utility layer cannot express.
# Testing

Robust testing is a hard requirement, and so is test-driven development. Applies to every change.

## Test first
- Red, green, refactor. Write the test, run it and watch it fail for the expected reason, write the least code that makes it pass, then clean up with the test still green. Run the red step in the session so the transcript shows it.
- Every commit is green. All suites that the change touches pass before `git commit`; a failing test is never committed. A commit holds the test and the code that passes it together.
- New behaviour gets a test in the same commit. A bug fix starts with a test that reproduces the bug.

## Each layer earns its place
Test a behaviour once, at the lowest layer that can catch it. A higher layer covers only what the lower layers cannot see. Before adding a test, name the failure it catches that no existing test catches; if there is none, do not add it.

| Layer | Tool | Owns | Does not re-test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backend unit | pytest | pure functions in the core: ordering, search filters, validation, token and password helpers | anything HTTP or SQL |
| Backend integration | pytest, httpx `ASGITransport`, a real database | each endpoint's contract: status codes, response shape, auth, ownership, persistence | the pure rules already unit-tested, beyond one case that proves the wiring |
| Frontend unit and component | Vitest (its API matches Jest's), React Testing Library, MSW at the `fetch` boundary | pure helpers, hooks, and each screen's states: loading, empty, error, success, validation | backend rules |
| Live-server e2e | pytest against the running stack (compose, then k3d) | what only a deployed stack shows: migrations ran, the proxy and cookie path, ingress and routing, a session issued by one replica accepted by another | endpoint contracts |
| Browser e2e | Playwright against the running stack | a few complete user journeys: sign in, create, reorder, search, edit, delete, sign out; and the small-screen layout | screen states and endpoint contracts |
| Load | k6 from its container against the running stack | latency and error budgets at 200 concurrent users, data consistency afterwards, and the round's capacity figure from a stepped run | correctness of single requests |

## Concurrency
- Each race in the spec has an integration test named after it that fires the requests together with `asyncio.TaskGroup` against a real Postgres. Each one must fail when its guard is removed; show that once, in the session.
- A fixture runs the backend suite in asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold and fails any test during which the event loop was blocked.
- The race tests and the load tests are run with the lead present: show the scripts and budgets first, then walk through the results.

## Mechanics
- Mock at the boundary (the HTTP client, `fetch`, the clock), never inside the code under test. Nothing in a unit suite opens a socket.
- Tests are independent and order-free. Each builds its own data through factories or fixtures; none relies on another's leftovers.
- Assert on behaviour a user or caller can see: status, body, rendered text and roles. Never on private attributes or CSS class names.
- One reason to fail per test. The name says the behaviour: `test_reorder_rejects_task_owned_by_another_user`, `it("shows the empty state when the user has no tasks")`.
- Coverage is a floor, not a target: CI fails below the threshold set in `pyproject.toml` and `vitest.config.ts`. A line covered by a test that asserts nothing is not covered.
- Report results as they are. "128 passed" means you saw it. Name the suite and the stack it ran against.

# API contract

The REST contract between `backend/` and `frontend/`. Change both sides in the same PR, or neither.

- Resources are nouns under `/api/v1`: `/auth/...`, `/tasks`, `/tasks/{id}`. Standard methods: `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PATCH` updates part of a resource, `DELETE` removes. JSON in and out.
- Status codes:

| Case | Code |
|---|---|
| Read or update succeeded | 200 |
| Created; the response carries the resource and a `Location` header | 201 |
| Deleted | 204, no body |
| Body or query fails validation | **400** (FastAPI's default is 422; the app maps `RequestValidationError` to 400 in one handler) |
| No token, bad token, expired token, wrong password | 401 |
| Authenticated but not allowed to do this action | 403 |
| Resource missing, **or owned by another user** (so ids of other users' tasks are never confirmed) | 404 |
| Conflict with current state, such as an email already registered | 409 |
| `If-Match` names an old version of the task | 412 |
| Overloaded (in-flight limit, no free database connection) or database unreachable | 503 |

- JSON field names are camelCase on the wire (`dueDate`, `createdAt`). Pydantic models use `alias_generator=to_camel` with `populate_by_name=True`; Python code keeps snake_case.
- Tasks carry an integer `version`, returned as the `ETag` header. `PATCH` honours `If-Match` (412 on mismatch) and changes only the fields sent.
- Every error body has one shape, a typed model: `{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "...", "details": [...]}}`. `code` is a stable machine string the frontend switches on; `message` is safe to show a user.
- List endpoints return a typed envelope, not a bare array, so paging can be added without breaking clients.
- The frontend parses every response with a Zod schema that mirrors the backend's Pydantic model. When a model changes, the schema changes in the same PR, and the integration test for that endpoint asserts the new shape.
- Every endpoint has an integration test for its success code and each error code it can return.

request ended the session again. Sign-out had the same lag, which made

mutations, so their progress and errors are still shared.

A late 401 that lands after the user is already on sign-in no longer
navigates again, which would wrap the way back in a second returnTo.

Review of feature/web-data-layer (PR D): 4 behaviour bugs I reproduced with probe tests, 1 security gap, 3 tests that can't fail. Gates are green: check, test (197/197) and build pass at HEAD, and every one of the 12 commits passes tsc, eslint and vitest on its own. I ran the probes and mutations in a scratch worktree, now removed; the review worktree is untouched.

FINDINGS, most severe first

1. HIGH (privacy). frontend/src/lib/query/tasks.ts:141-149, 180-183, 222-224. A 401 on a toggle, move or delete leaves the previous user's tasks in the cache. TanStack runs the global onError (client.clear() and go to sign-in) before the hook's own onError, and restoreLists then puts the snapshot back. Probe: after the 401, `["tasks","list",{q:""}]` held all 8 tasks. If a second person signs in on that browser within the 5-minute gcTime, they see the first user's titles until the refetch lands. Fix: skip the rollback when `error.code === not_authenticated`, in one shared helper.

I reproduced four behaviour bugs with probe tests, found one gap in the `returnTo` check, and found three test gaps where breaking the guarded code leaves every test green. The gates are green: check, test (197/197) and build pass at HEAD, and each of the 12 commits passes typecheck, lint and tests on its own.

**Findings, most severe first** (all in `frontend/src/lib/query/tasks.ts` unless noted)
1. **High (privacy):** a 401 on a toggle, move or delete leaves the previous user's tasks in the cache (lines 141-149, 180-183, 222-224). The global 401 handler clears the cache before each hook's own error handler runs, and that handler then puts its snapshot back. The probe found all 8 tasks still cached after the 401. Fix: skip the rollback on `not_authenticated`.
2. **Medium:** a list refetch can land between queued moves. Toggle, delete and create reload the lists every time they finish (lines 151, 200, 225). The probe ran two queued moves plus a tick: the list jumped back to its original order until the queue finished. Fix: skip that reload while a move is pending.
3. **Medium:** a failed background refetch throws away an unsaved edit (line 40). The probe got a 500 on refocus during an edit: the error screen replaced the page and the unsaved title was lost. Fix: only send the error to the error screen when nothing is cached yet.
4. **Medium (security):** `/\t/evil.com` (and the `\n`, `\r` forms) gets past the `returnTo` check in `frontend/src/lib/schema/route.ts:5`, and the browser resolves it to evil.com. The sign-in redirect currently fails closed only because the redirect replaces the history entry. React Router's push falls back to `location.assign` when it is blocked, so any later push to `returnTo` is an open redirect.
5. **Medium:** a dismissed notice comes back after the user opens a task and returns to the list (lines 286, 310). The probe confirmed it.
6. **Low:** a save can be overwritten by an older refetch that was still in flight. I found this by reading the code, not with a probe.
7. **Low:** rolling back an earlier queued move also undoes later moves' on-screen positions until the final reload.

**Tests** (checked by breaking the code in a scratch worktree)
- These tests do fail when their behaviour breaks: the reorder race, the toggle rollback, the search abort, and the 412.
- Removing any of these still leaves every test passing:
  - the `cancelQueries` call before the optimistic write;
  - the check that only the last queued move reloads the lists;
  - the move rollback and the move 404 handling;
  - the delete rollback.
- "restores the task when delete fails" starts on the detail page with no list cached, so it cannot catch a broken rollback.

- `If-Match` is sent as `"<n>"` and the server's error codes are a closed list. There is no backend code on the base branch yet, so I couldn't check either against real code.
